nodes_source.source_quote: The data used to support the results of this study are available from the corresponding author upon request.
nodes_source.description: Vehicle locations extracted from traffic video frames and reformed as position matrices. Used as inputs for a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) method for ramp metering in a real-world case study. The data covers a road network including an on-ramp, upstream and downstream mainlines, and a merging area.
nodes_source.reproducibility_rationale: Data is available from the corresponding author upon request, no public link provided.

nodes_process.source_quote: The proposed method is evaluated in SUMO, an open-source microscopic traffic simulator [31]. [...] The simulation parameters regarding driving behaviors are calibrated based on empirical data.
nodes_process.description: A microscopic traffic simulator (SUMO) is used to set up a freeway environment based on a real-world location (Qingdao and Huangdao, China). This includes a one-lane on-ramp and a three-lane mainline. Simulation parameters for driving behaviors are calibrated using empirical data.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=3, some parameters stated; specific empirical data and calibration process details are missing.

nodes_process.node_name: Simulated Video Preprocessing and State Representation
nodes_process.source_quote: Vehicle locations are extracted from the traffic video frames and are reformed as position matrices. [...] After zooming and down-sampling, the size of one observation is 4x512 in pixels. Three consecutive observations are stacked to represent the traffic state.
nodes_process.description: Vehicle locations are extracted from simulated traffic video frames. These locations are used to form position matrices (size 4x512 pixels after zooming and down-sampling). Consecutive matrices (three) are then stacked to create the traffic state representation for the DRL method. Down-sampling reduces input dimensions.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=3, some parameters stated; specific vehicle extraction method and down-sampling details are missing.

nodes_process.source_quote: To accommodate the input size for ramp metering, the Q-network in Mnih et al. [30] is revised as Figure 7, which consists of three convolutional neural network (CNN) layers and one full connection (FC) layer for each output layer.
nodes_process.description: A Deep Q-network (Q-network) architecture is defined, adapted from Mnih et al. [30]. It features three convolutional neural network (CNN) layers followed by fully connected (FC) layers. Two separate FC output layers are used for multitask learning: one for Q-value estimation and another for predicting mean speed and queue length.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, all tools and parameters are named with specific values.

nodes_process.source_quote: The process of learning policy from the action-value function Q is termed Q-learning. The key step in Q-learning is to estimate Q* (s, a). [...] The algorithm for training the ramp metering policy is presented in Algorithm 1.
nodes_process.description: The Q-network is trained using a deep Q-learning algorithm to learn an optimal ramp metering policy. Adam optimizer is used for weight updates. Training stability is enhanced by experience replay and a target network. A multitask learning approach simultaneously predicts Q-values, mean speed, and queue length.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, all tools named, most parameters stated; number of training episodes not specified.

nodes_process.source_quote: The PI-ALINEA method fixes the length of the green phase and determines the length of the red phase in the current signal cycle based on the length of the red phase in the previous cycle and the downstream occupancies in the previous and current cycles.
nodes_process.description: The PI-ALINEA method is defined as a baseline. It uses a proportional-integral feedback control mechanism to determine the ramp metering rate (rk) based on previous rates and downstream mainline occupancies. It aims to keep occupancy at a predefined target value, with specified regulator parameters (KR, Kp) and a fixed green phase length.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, all required tools are named, and all parameters are stated.

nodes_process.source_quote: each scenario is evaluated in 20 simulation experiments. The simulations for the training phase and each experiment are initialized with different random seeds.
nodes_process.description: The trained DRL model, the PI-ALINEA method, and a no-control scenario are evaluated in 20 simulation experiments each, using the calibrated SUMO environment. Simulations are initialized with different random seeds. Metrics such as mean vehicle travel times, queue lengths, and traffic flows are collected and compared.

Intel Xeon CPU E5-1650 (3.6 GHz, 6 cores)
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, all tools mentioned, number of experiments stated; specific random seed values not provided.

nodes_process.source_quote: A perturbation analysis is conducted to evaluate the impact of information contained in video data. [...] The information in the subarea is removed from original data to generate perturbed data for each subarea. The impact of missing information for each subarea is evaluated in 20 simulation experiments with perturbed data.
nodes_process.description: A perturbation analysis is performed to assess the DRL method's sensitivity to video data information. The control area is conceptually divided into eight subareas. Information from each subarea is individually removed from the simulated input data to create perturbed datasets. The DRL model's performance (travel times) is then re-evaluated for each perturbed dataset in 20 simulation experiments.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, method described, number of subareas and runs stated; specific details on 'information removal' could be more explicit.

nodes_sink.source_quote: FIGURE 8: Convergence curves for (a) episode reward and (b) mean travel time.

nodes_sink.reproducibility_rationale: Training parameters (Table 1) are stated, but training data and code are not open. The plots visually support the reported convergence.

nodes_sink.source_quote: FIGURE 9: Vehicle travel times in the mainline.
nodes_sink.description: Compares vehicle travel times in the mainline for three scenarios: no control, PI-ALINEA, and Deep RL. Shows median and interquartile ranges over time.
nodes_sink.reproducibility_rationale: SUMO is open-source, but full simulation setup and code are not provided. The figure coherently shows the comparison of travel times.

nodes_sink.source_quote: TABLE 2: Mean travel times in 20 simulation experiments (s).
nodes_sink.description: Presents mean vehicle travel times in seconds for 20 simulation experiments under no control, PI-ALINEA, and DRL methods, including percentage change from no control.
nodes_sink.reproducibility_rationale: Based on 20 SUMO simulations, but full configuration for each run (e.g., random seeds) is not provided. Values are coherent with claims.

nodes_sink.source_quote: FIGURE 10: Temporal-spatial distribution of speed in (a) no-control; (b) PI-ALINEA; (c) DRL.

nodes_sink.reproducibility_rationale: Based on SUMO simulations, but full configuration is not provided. The plots show the claimed speed distributions.

nodes_sink.reproducibility_rationale: Based on SUMO simulations, but full configuration is not provided. The figure coherently presents the queue length comparisons.

nodes_sink.source_quote: FIGURE 12: Relationship of queue length and red ratio for (a) PI-ALINEA and (b) DRL.

nodes_sink.reproducibility_rationale: Based on SUMO simulation outputs. Details on deriving red ratio and exact plotting methods are not fully explicit.
